newsitem.title: ITALY: Benetton ponders its cash pile.
newsitem.headline: Benetton ponders its cash pile.

text.p: Italy's Benetton, often plunged into controversy by its stark advertising campaigns, is facing a more enviable problem than fending off criticism: what to do with all the cash it is making.

Later this month, when the company reports its 1996 results, Benetton is set to confirm that the company eliminated its debt and ended the year with net cash in the bank. This cash is likely to grow substantially this year and in following years.
An acquisition could be trickly to absorb into Benetton's unique system of manufacturing, commissioned agents and licensed retail outlets, so other plans are under consideration.
Benetton's managing director, Carlo Gilardi, says this net cash must have a return, and must be used to the advantage of Benetton Group's minority shareholders.
"An acquisition will be done -- but only if the acquisition has the same prospects as that of the Benetton company," he said in an interview at the group's headquarters in northeast Italy.

Analysts believe that returns to minority shareholders can be improved by either increasing the dividend or by stock buybacks. The Benetton family company, Edizione Holding, holds a 71.3 percent stake in the Benetton Group, with the remaining shares listed on the Milan stock exchange.

Benetton tried a stock buyback of 2 million shares, or 1.2 percent of shares, last year costing 33 billion lire ($19 million) -- but further scope seems limited for liquidity reasons with just over 28 percent of shares floated.

Some analysts see Benetton's 1996 dividend being lifted to 500 lire (29 cents) per share from 425 lire (24 cents) in 1995, but, even with this double-digit growth in dividends until the end of the century, cash could still build up in Benetton's bank account.

Benetton has spent 200 billion lire ($117 million) in the last three years at its Castrette "technology village" close to its headquarters at Ponzano on new textile factories and technology upgrades, and further immediate heavy capital spending is now limited.
But, despite the strong underlying financial performance of the group, Gilardi still sees the shares as undervalued. So why are they not performing better?

Analysts say the financial market is clearly concerned that the Benetton family company Edizione could look to use Benetton cash for its more financially stretched operations -- such as Benetton Sportsystem, GS supermarkets and Autogrill.
Top of its list of concerns is for Edizione to sell its 100 percent-owned Benetton Sportsystem to Benetton Group at an inflated price. But Gilardi is adamant this will not happen.

"If this acquisition was not at the right price, then Benetton's stock will fall and that would hurt Edizione," he said. Gilardi says an acquisition is under consideration as with a number of other plans but says nothing is planned.
"There are some synergies with Benetton Sportsystem as it contains some exciting brands. We would not exclude looking inside Benetton Sportsystem to maximize any synergies."

Benetton Sportsystem boasts a number of leading sports brands such as Prince tennis rackets, Nordica ski boots, Rollerblade in-line skates, Kastle skis and bycyles, Killer Loop sportswear and Asolo mountain boots. It has global sales of 1.4 trillion lire ($821 million), with 54 percent generated in America.
Gilardi emphasises that if an acquisition was planned, the price of Benetton Sportsystem would be independently assessed.

Analysts say Benetton is a victim of its own success spending heavily on technology and keeping its work force at a modest 6,000 due by extensive subcontracting while it has not any financial interest in its 7,000 licensed retail outlets.

The group has grown rapidly in its 32-year history since Luciano Benetton and his brothers and sister founded the company. It has become the world's biggest buyer of processed wool, makes 8 million garments a year and virtually singlehandedly created a textile industry in the northeast Veneto region of Italy.
Analysts believe an increased Benetton dividend is most likely to keep its minority shareholders happy and Edizione as the largest shareholder of Benetton is likely to approve.
